cases.authorIntent: A 41-year-old who has never run builds from nothing to a 10K over 16 weeks with bodyweight-only running-support strength, a Wednesday start in a negative time zone, and one fully declared nonclinical week off. It probes whether the coach starts with walk/jog, progresses gradually, absorbs a short break without catching up, and lands a taper and race week on the stated date.

interruption.reason: Work trip all week, no time to train.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: A complete, in-scope intake with a race 15+ weeks away is plannable; no fact is missing.
Someone with zero running history should start with walk/jog (or walking), not continuous running.
No harder running sessions in the first month for a complete beginner.
The race falls on day 4 of week 15.
The goal race is part of the plan on its date.

assert.statement: Every strength exercise in every week is executable with bodyweight only (no implement or machine), and every strength load is BODYWEIGHT.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: Equipment is bodyweight only; the repertoire must stay within it.

assert.statement: Runs appear only on days 0, 2 and 4 and strength only on days 1 and 5 of each week; no other day receives a session.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: Chosen days belong to the athlete; no session on an unchosen day.

assert.statement: Running load grows gradually from walk/jog toward continuous easy running; no single week shows an abrupt jump in total running time, and the longest session never exceeds the 75 minutes available on the long-run day.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: Gradual progression is the central safety property for a novice.
A fully declared 7-day nonclinical break needs no question; the coach re-plans or keeps.
All week-7 sessions are covered by the declared break, so nothing is unknown.
Nothing is pending after a declared nonclinical break.

assert.statement: The first week back (week 8) does not exceed the running load of the last completed week before the break (week 6) and does not try to catch up the missed week; a small step back or a repeat of week 6 is appropriate.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: One missed week in a beginner means resume, not compensate.
The race week stays in place after the last pre-race review.
The race stays prescribed on its date.

assert.statement: Running in the final 7-10 days before the race is reduced relative to the peak weeks, with no new or harder session types introduced in race week, and strength in race week is light or absent in the two days before the race.

expectedDomainProperties.rationale: A short taper suits a novice 10K.

metamorphicRelations.rationale: The same 7-day break declared with a different nonclinical reason category (VACATION instead of WORK) should produce the same return plan; the category only matters for the clinical/nonclinical split. (Direction: the variant's plan compared with the base case's plan.)
The Wednesday start and negative offset are central: day offsets, not weekday names, define the week.

independentAssessment.rationale: A true beginner (no running at all, novice strength) aiming at a 10K in 16 weeks. This is feasible as a completion goal with run/walk progressions. The risks are starting with continuous running, progressing too fast, adding intensity early, or reacting to a missed week by compressing the build.
independentAssessment.preferredCoachingBehavior: Start with walk/jog intervals three times per week totalling a modest amount of time, progress the run fraction and duration a little each week, keep all running easy until continuous easy running is established (quality, if any, only late and gentle such as strides or short steady segments), build a longer session on the Sunday up to roughly 60-75 minutes of running or run/walk, taper in the last 7-10 days, race on the date. Strength: two short bodyweight sessions (squat, hinge, lunge, calf, push, pull/trunk patterns) with high reps in reserve. After the declared work week off: resume at or slightly below the week-6 level.
acceptableAlternatives: A plan whose last weeks still contain short walk breaks so the race can be completed as run/walk.
Starting with WALK sessions only for the first week before walk/jog.
Keeping strength to one session a week during the taper.
Repeating week 6 exactly after the break.
concerns: Continuous 30-40 minute runs in week 0 (uses the time available rather than the current capacity).
Quality or threshold work in the first month.
A week after the break that is harder than before it, or doubling sessions to make up for the lost week.
A long session that exceeds 75 minutes, or runs on strength days.
Asking a question after a fully declared nonclinical break.

cases.domainNotes: Asking is not needed anywhere in this timeline: every week is reported and the break is declared with a nonclinical category. The time zone is UTC-05:00; step clocks are local. The race is on the long-run day so the race reference is unambiguous.

independentAssessment.rationale: A well-prepared intermediate runner with a credible half-marathon goal and an experienced lifter who only wants to keep strength. The interesting part is the unreported peak week right before the taper: the coach cannot know whether the athlete absorbed the peak, so it should ask before setting taper doses, and a late answer should land the athlete exactly where an on-time review would have.
independentAssessment.preferredCoachingBehavior: Plan four runs (easy, quality, easy, long on Sunday) with two maintenance strength sessions on Friday and Monday using known loads at lower volume. Build the long run toward roughly 105-125 minutes by week 7-8, taper from week 9 (shorter long run, maintained but reduced quality, lower volume), race on Sunday of week 10 with a short sharpening session and a shakeout before it, then an easy post-race week. At the start of week 9, ask about the unreported week-8 runs; after the answer, confirm or re-plan the taper and keep Monday of week 9 empty.
acceptableAlternatives: A 7-day taper (taper starts only in race week) if the peak long run is placed in week 8.
Keeping one short strength session in race week early in the week.
Strides in the post-race week.
Treating the unreported week conservatively without asking only if the taper doses were not increased; asking is better.
concerns: Assuming the unreported peak week was done and silently keeping the projection.
Moving the Monday session of week 9 to Tuesday or Wednesday on an unchosen day.
A long run or heavy squats in the two days before the race.
Quality sessions in the week after the race.
Resetting the experienced lifter to ESTABLISH loads.

cases.authorIntent: A strength-first athlete with only kettlebells, a pull-up bar and bodyweight at home, and little running, changes her training days mid-program and then travels for a week to a hotel gym with different equipment, then returns home. It probes equipment-bound exercise selection, known kettlebell loads and conventions, schedule changes, a temporary equipment window, and a local lower-body fatigue signal.

cases.authorIntent: A formerly experienced runner restarts from 20 minutes a week after five months off, then mid-program signs up for a 10K, and later the race is moved two weeks earlier. It probes that past experience does not override current capacity, that a shortened but tolerated run is not treated as intolerance, and that goal and event-date changes re-plan without compressing load.

independentAssessment.rationale: Past experience helps the rate of progression but the starting point must be today's capacity: 20 minutes a week. The moved race shortens the time to prepare; the right reaction is a shorter build and taper, not a steeper ramp.
independentAssessment.preferredCoachingBehavior: Start with three short easy runs (e.g., 15-25 minutes), progress about 10-20% per week with a step-back week, add strides then gentle threshold work only after ~3-4 weeks, long run on Saturday growing from ~25 to ~60-75 minutes. On the goal change, plan toward the 10K from the current level. On the date change, re-plan with the taper starting about 7-10 days before the new date and a post-race easy week, without raising the weekly load.

Quality in the first two weeks.
Reducing load after the time-limited shortened run.
Increasing volume steeply after the race moves earlier.
Leaving the race on the old date or racing twice.

A return week with only easy runs and a single strength session.

concerns: Planning a return at r5 from the free text.
Resuming at the pre-illness level after clearance.

A marathon three weeks away is out of scope and also a bad idea for a novice runner.

concerns: Reducing the run plan after the heat-confounded long run.
Accelerating strength progression for the rest of the program as a learned trait.
Building any marathon or long-distance plan.
Dropping the existing plan after the rejected request.
